newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Afghan rebels say capture last east province.
newsitem.headline: Afghan rebels say capture last east province.

text.p: Afghanistan's rebel Taleban Islamic militia said on Sunday it had captured the last pro-government eastern province of Kunar, bordering Pakistan, after heavy fighting.

Taleban sources, quoted by a Pakistan-based private Afghan news service, said the militia seized the provincial capital Asadabad on Saturday night after heavy fighting on the way in a district of the adjoining Nangarhar province.

There was no immediate confirmation of the report by the Afghan government, which has suffered a series of reverses this month in eastern Afghanistan, including the fall of strategic Nangarhar and Laghman provinces.
Kunar was governed by a fundamentalist Islamic group called Salfis, whose leader Maulvi Samiullah Najabi is the minister for mines and disabled in Prime Minister Gulbuddin Hekmatyar's cabinet.

Heavy fighting had raged between Taleban and fighters of Hekmatyar's Hezb-e-Islami faction in Shewa, about 25 km (16 miles) north of Jalalabad, since Friday as the militia sought to advance from there to Asadabad, AIP said.
There were no immediate details about fighting at Asadabad, which Afghan sources said was poorly defended.
AIP quoted Taleban as saying its forces had seized many tanks, artillery and other weapons.

The Taleban advance on Kunar followed failure of several days of talks with the defenders on surrender terms after the militia seized Nangarhar and Laghman provinces without much fighting in a drive to capture maximum territory in the war- shattered country.
The militia, which now controls more than half of Afghanistan, aims to overthrow President Burhanuddin Rabbani's government in Kabul and install a purist Islamic order throughout the country.
On Saturday, Taleban urged pro-government fighters to defect to its side and promised them amnesty.

Mullah Amir Khan Mutaqi, a Taleban spokesman at the southern Afghan town of Kandahar, told Reuters by telephone that movement leader Mullah Mohammad Omar had announced amnesty for commanders and fighters of various factions, civil servants and citizens.
"Those who join us would be provided complete protection of their lives and properties," he quoted Omar as saying.
The latest Taleban sweep has soured relations again between Islamabad and Kabul, which accuses Pakistan of aiding the rebels.
Pakistan denies the charges and says it has no favourites among the warring factions, most of which it helped during their guerrilla war against Soviet occupation in the 1980s.
Taleban has also besieged Kabul since last October to force Rabbani's government to step down.
